title: The relational model: tables, primary and foreign keys

videos.script: Almost everybody's first database is a spreadsheet. One sheet, one row per thing, and for a while it works perfectly. {{sheet}} Then somebody asks a question. Which customers ordered twice last month and never came back. And you find that the sheet cannot answer it — not because the data is missing, but because of how it was arranged. {{question}} Here is what went wrong, and it went wrong on the very first day. The customer's name is written on every one of their orders. Forty orders, forty copies of one name. {{repeated}} Now the name is wrong on one of them. Which one is the real customer? The sheet has no opinion. It never had one, because it was never asked to keep track of what a customer IS — only of what each row says. {{no-opinion}} The relational model is what somebody invented instead, and the whole of it is one idea: a customer is recorded once, in one place, and everything else points at it. {{once}} That sounds small. It is the reason a database can answer a question nobody thought of when the data was written down — which is the thing a spreadsheet can never do, and the thing you are here to learn. {{title}}
